description: Query optimization decomposed. Statistics (histograms, MCV), selectivity estimation, join order enumeration (DP, genetic, greedy), index selection, predicate pushdown, join reordering, materialized view rewriting. The mechanisms by which databases turn SQL into fast plans.

sub_mechanisms.name: table_statistics
sub_mechanisms.definition: Per-column: row count, distinct values, null fraction, MCVs (most-common values), histogram of distribution.
sub_mechanisms.why: Drives all cost estimates. Selectivity (fraction of rows matching predicate) computed from stats. Stale stats give wrong selectivity → wrong plans. ANALYZE refreshes.

sub_mechanisms.name: histogram_estimation
sub_mechanisms.definition: Equi-depth or equi-width histogram of column values. Estimates selectivity of range predicates (col > X).
sub_mechanisms.why: Continuous-value predicates need distribution data. Histogram bucket containing X gives estimated fraction. Postgres default: 100 buckets per column; adjustable.

sub_mechanisms.name: most_common_values_MCV
sub_mechanisms.definition: List of frequently-occurring values + their frequencies. Selectivity of col = X uses MCV if X is in list; histogram otherwise.
sub_mechanisms.why: Skewed distributions (e.g., status column with 95% 'OK', 5% spread across other values). MCV captures the spike; histogram captures the tail. Together: accurate selectivity for any X.

sub_mechanisms.name: join_selectivity
sub_mechanisms.definition: Estimated rows output by join. For equality join: rows_left × rows_right / max(distinct_left, distinct_right).
sub_mechanisms.why: Drives join order decisions. Output size determines next join's input size. Bad join selectivity → cascading bad estimates.

sub_mechanisms.name: join_order_DP
sub_mechanisms.definition: Dynamic programming over subsets of joining tables. Computes optimal plan for each subset; combines. O(3^n) for n tables.
sub_mechanisms.why: Optimal up to ~12 tables. Tractable thanks to subset DP. Postgres uses this for ≤ geqo_threshold; falls back to genetic for more.

sub_mechanisms.name: genetic_query_optimisation
sub_mechanisms.definition: For large joins (>12 tables): genetic algorithm. Population of join orders; mutate + crossover + select.
sub_mechanisms.why: DP doesn't scale to 20+ tables. Genetic gives 'pretty good' plans for large joins. Postgres geqo. Sometimes finds worse plans than DP — tradeoff for tractability.

sub_mechanisms.name: predicate_pushdown
sub_mechanisms.definition: Move filtering predicates closer to data source. WHERE clause applied before join when possible.
sub_mechanisms.why: Reduces intermediate result size. Filter 1M rows down to 1000 before joining; far cheaper than join then filter. Standard rule-based optimisation.

sub_mechanisms.name: constant_folding_QP
sub_mechanisms.definition: Evaluate constant expressions at plan time: WHERE x > 5 + 3 → WHERE x > 8.
sub_mechanisms.why: Same compiler optimisation applied to SQL. Predicate becomes simpler; sometimes opens further opts (constant-vs-constant becomes always-true/false).

sub_mechanisms.name: subquery_unnesting
sub_mechanisms.definition: Transform correlated subquery into join. EXISTS becomes semi-join; IN becomes hash-join.
sub_mechanisms.why: Naive correlated subquery: re-execute for each outer row. Unnested: one pass. 10-1000x speedup common. Major Postgres + commercial DB optimisation.

sub_mechanisms.name: common_subexpression_elimination_QP
sub_mechanisms.definition: Same subquery appearing twice computed once. WITH CTE materialised once + referenced.
sub_mechanisms.why: Postgres 12+ inlines CTEs by default but can MATERIALIZED. Optimisation analogous to compiler CSE. Important for complex analytical queries.

sub_mechanisms.name: materialized_view_rewriting
sub_mechanisms.definition: Optimizer recognises that a query matches a materialised view; substitutes view scan for original computation.
sub_mechanisms.why: Snowflake, BigQuery, Oracle all do this. Auto-rewrite without app changes. Foundation of automatic aggregation pre-computation. Hot research area.

sub_mechanisms.name: plan_caching
sub_mechanisms.definition: Cache compiled execution plans for repeated queries. Skip planning on next execution.
sub_mechanisms.why: Planning can dominate cost for simple queries. Cache key: SQL text + parameter types. Most OLTP databases (Postgres prepared statements, SQL Server plan cache) do this.

derivation_rules.name: selectivity_estimation_dominates_plan_quality
if: selectivity estimates are off by factor F
then: join orders downstream cascade errors growing as F^n for n joins
derivation_rules.why: Each estimated output feeds next plan's cost. Compound errors blow up exponentially. Worst case: chose hash join when nested loop would have been better — orders of magnitude slowdown.

derivation_rules.name: predicate_pushdown_reduces_intermediate_size
if: a filter applies to one table in a join
then: pushing it before the join reduces work
derivation_rules.why: Filter 1M rows → 100 rows then join 100 vs filter 100 from 1M-row join result. The former does linear filter + small join; the latter does big join + linear filter. Same predicate; orders-of-magnitude perf difference.

derivation_rules.name: histogram_essential_for_range_predicates
if: predicate is range-based (col > X) on skewed data
then: histogram is required for accurate selectivity
derivation_rules.why: Without histogram: uniform assumption gives wrong estimates on skewed data. With histogram: bucket-based estimate captures distribution. Postgres + commercial DBs all use histograms.

derivation_rules.name: join_order_DP_optimal_for_small_n
derivation_rules.why: Computational cost ~3^n. Tractable until ~12. Beyond: switch to genetic or other heuristic. Most queries have few enough tables; large analytical queries use genetic.

derivation_rules.name: plan_caching_amortises_planning_cost
then: cached plan eliminates per-execution planning cost
derivation_rules.why: Planning can take ms; execution can take µs (point lookup). Cached plan = constant overhead. Critical for OLTP. Postgres prepared statements, MySQL binary protocol use this.
